questions.stem: Which of the following is not an amphipathic lipid?
questions.solutionHtml:
Triglyceride
  • An amphipathic lipid is a lipid molecule that has both hydrophilic (water-attracting) and hydrophobic (water-repelling) regions. This property allows them to align themselves to form various structures in water environments such as cell membranes.
  • A Triglycerides: Triglycerides are a type of fat that is found in the blood. A triglyceride molecule is composed of a glycerol backbone and three fatty acid chains. All of these parts are hydrophobic, meaning they are not attracted to water. Hence, triglycerides are not considered amphipathic lipids because they do not have a hydrophilic portion.


Harper 30th e/p 257

questions.stem: Which of the following is not Glucogenic?
questions.solutionHtml:
Acetyl CoA
  • Acetyl CoA: This is a two-carbon molecule that is an intermediate in many biochemical pathways. While it is vital for energy production through the citric acid cycle (also known as the Krebs cycle or TCA cycle), it cannot be used to generate glucose because of irreversible nature of link reaction. Therefore, it is not considered glucogenic but instead is classified as ketogenic.


Harper 30th e/p 171

questions.stem: Wobble hypothesis is due to which property of codon?
questions.solutionHtml:
Degeneracy

The wobble hypothesis is related to the property of "degeneracy" of the genetic code.

  • Degeneracy: This refers to the fact that multiple codons (sequences of three nucleotides) can code for the same amino acid.
  • This is the reason for the "wobble" effect, where the first two nucleotides of the codon are often more critical for determining the amino acid, and the third nucleotide can "wobble" or vary without changing the amino acid that is produced.


Lehninger’s 7th /e p1084 fig 27-8]

questions.stem: Which is more appropriate for the quantitative analysis of viral RNA genome

options.label: B
options.text: Conventional PCR with restriction fragment length pair technique

options.label: D
options.text: RT-PCR followed by real time PCR

questions.answerText: RT-PCR followed by real time PCR
questions.solutionHtml:
RT-PCR followed by real time PCR
  • The most appropriate method for the quantitative analysis of a viral RNA genome is RT-PCR followed by real-time PCR. This technique, often called quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR), uses RT-PCR to first convert RNA into cDNA.
  • The cDNA is then quantified using real-time PCR. This allows for the quantitative analysis of RNA, including RNA from viral genomes. This method is very sensitive and can quantify very small amounts of RNA, making it a preferred method for such applications.


Lehninger’s 6th/e pg. 331

Nonhomologous end joining
  • The CRISPR-Cas9 system, when used for genome editing, induces double-strand breaks in DNA. These breaks are then repaired by the cell's own repair machinery. Two of the main pathways for repairing double-strand breaks in DNA are:
    • Homology Directed Repair (HDR)
    • Nonhomologous End Joining (NHEJ)
  • HDR is an accurate repair process that uses a template (usually supplied by the researcher in a laboratory setting) to repair the break, while NHEJ is a quicker, but more error-prone process that directly ligates the broken ends together, often introducing small insertions or deletions.
  • The options given are all DNA repair mechanisms, but only one, c) Nonhomologous End Joining, is typically involved in repairing the double-strand breaks introduced by the CRISPR-Cas9 system.

questions.stem: True about mitochondrial DNAHigher chances of mutation as compared to nuclear genomeSingle stranded circular DNAMitochondrial codons are slightly different from nuclear DNA codonsMitochondrial DNA encodes for all ETC complex proteinHas around 16,000 base pairsSelect the correct answer from the given below code:-
questions.solutionHtml:
A, C, E

Let’s explore all the options:

  • Option A. Higher chances of mutation as compared to the nuclear genome: True. mtDNA is more prone to mutations than nuclear DNA due to a lack of introns, less efficient DNA repair mechanisms, and its proximity to reactive oxygen species (ROS) produced by the electron transport chain.
  • Option B. Single stranded circular DNA: False. Mitochondrial DNA in most animals, including humans, is double-stranded and circular.
  • Option C. Mitochondrial codons are slightly different from nuclear DNA codons: True. The genetic code of mtDNA does indeed have some differences compared to the universal genetic code used in nuclear DNA. For example, in human mitochondria, UGA codes for tryptophan instead of serving as a stop codon, and AUA codes for methionine instead of isoleucine.
  • Option D. Mitochondrial DNA encodes for all Electron Transport Chain (ETC) complex proteins: False. mtDNA does not encode all the proteins required for the ETC. In humans, the mitochondrial genome encodes 13 proteins, all of which are subunits of the enzyme complexes involved in oxidative phosphorylation. The rest of the proteins involved in the ETC are encoded by nuclear genes and are imported into the mitochondria after being synthesized in the cytosol.
  • Option E. Has around 16,000 base pairs: True. The mitochondrial genome is much smaller than the nuclear genome. In humans, it is a circular DNA molecule approximately 16.6 kilobases in size.


Harper 30th e/p 378

PDH
  • Thiamine, in its active form as Thiamine Pyrophosphate (TPP), acts as a coenzyme for several enzymes involved in carbohydrate metabolism. Among the options given:
    • PDH (Pyruvate Dehydrogenase): True. TPP is an essential coenzyme for the PDH complex, which catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, a critical step in the metabolic pathway for glucose.


Harper 30th e/p 164

questions.stem: Which of the following is false in advanced liver disease?

options.label: B
options.text: Increase synthesis of glutamate and glutamine from alpha-ketoglutarate

questions.solutionHtml:
Oxidative decarboxylation of alpha ketoglutarate
  • In the context of advanced liver disease, urea cycle is affected as liver is the only organ where this cycle occurs. The consequences are increased ammonia:
  • Oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-ketoglutarate: This is a reaction in the citric acid cycle (also known as the Krebs cycle or TCA cycle) where alpha-ketoglutarate is converted to succinyl-CoA. Advanced liver disease doesn't typically inhibits this specific reaction.
  • Given the explanations above, the statement a) "Oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-ketoglutarate" is the least directly related to changes observed in advanced liver disease, making it the most likely to be the false statement in this context.


Lehninger’s 7th/e pg. 686, 687

questions.stemHtml: A patient came to hospital who has not eaten anything for two days which of the following test will be positive?
questions.solutionHtml:
Only C
  • When a patient has been fasting or not eating for an extended period, their body starts to utilize stored forms of energy. Glycogen stored in the liver is one of the first energy sources to be used, but it's typically depleted within 24 hours. After this, the body begins to break down fats for energy. This process produces ketone bodies, which can accumulate in the blood and urine.
  • Among the tests listed:


Harper 30th e/p 232

Ion exchange chromatography
  • Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) is an important biomarker used to monitor long-term glucose control in individuals with diabetes. It represents the amount of glucose that has been irreversibly bound to the hemoglobin in red blood cells over their lifespan (about 120 days). The HbA1c level reflects the average blood glucose concentration over the previous 2-3 months.
  • Among the methods listed for HbA1c measurement:
  • On exchange chromatography: This is a commonly used method and is considered a reference method for HbA1c determination. It separates hemoglobins based on their charge differences. HbA1c has a different charge than other forms of hemoglobin, which allows it to be separated and quantified.

questions.stem: Which requires maximum energy for assimilation
questions.solutionHtml:
Proteins
  • Assimilation refers to the processes by which the body digests and absorbs nutrients from food, converting them into usable forms. One measure of the energy used in these processes is the thermic effect of food (TEF) or dietary induced thermogenesis, which is the amount of energy expended above the resting metabolic rate due to the cost of processing food for storage and use.
  • Option A. Proteins: Among the macronutrients, proteins have the highest TEF. This means that the body uses more energy to digest, absorb, and assimilate protein compared to fats and carbohydrates.


Harper’s 31st/e pg. 524
